draft_text:
Hans Poelzig designed Babylon as part of a housing block on what was then Bülowplatz, a wedge of Neue Sachlichkeit geometry completed in 1929 — the same year the Weimar Republic began its final, vertiginous slide. The cinema held 1,200 seats in a single hall, survived the war when almost nothing around it did, became a GDR speciality house, nearly collapsed, and was rebuilt behind its original façade for the twenty-first century. It is the kind of venue that accumulates historical irony the way old walls accumulate paint. So there is something quietly apt about an Irish film festival taking up residence here each March: two cultures that know a thing or two about partition, reconstruction, and the stubborn afterlife of the past.

Irish Film Berlin — running its [~fourth edition from 13 to 18 March 2026|the festival's own site and press materials give conflicting counts, calling it both the "third" and "fourth" time; programme dates confirm six screening days across nearly a week~] — is a small festival by any metric. It has no industry market, no jury prizes with engraved statuettes, no red carpet snaking down Rosa-Luxemburg-Straße. What it does have is a tightly curated programme, an official partnership with the Irish Film Institute's IFI International programme, and the good fortune of existing during a period when Irish screen talent operates at an almost absurd level of global visibility. Cillian Murphy's Oppenheimer Oscar is barely two years old. Paul Mescal has gone from Normal People to Gladiator to something approaching ubiquity. Barry Keoghan has turned a career of feral, off-kilter performances into genuine star power. The pipeline from Ireland to the centre of world cinema has never been shorter or wider, and a festival like this gets to ride that current while also doing something the mainstream moment cannot: showing the films the algorithm will never surface.

The programme this year turns its regional lens on Dublin and the East, after previous editions spotlighted the Midlands, the Midwest, and the North. Friday opens with Girls and Boys, a feature about a trans filmmaker and a rugby player meeting at a Dublin college party — the kind of contemporary queer Irish narrative that would have been almost unthinkable in Irish cinema a generation ago, when the country's relationship to sexuality was still tangled in Church doctrine and criminal law. That it screens in the same slot as Intermission, John Crowley's chaotic 2003 Dublin ensemble piece starring a then-unknown Murphy and Colin Farrell, sets up a productive dialogue across two decades of the city's self-image on screen.

Saturday's programme brings a short film selection called Spice Bag — named, presumably, after the chip-shop dish that has become a minor national obsession — and includes Snot Rocket, shot in Schöneberg, about two Irish immigrants who decide to rob an old bookstore. The detail matters: an Irish film set in Berlin, screening in Berlin, at a festival that exists precisely because there is a large enough Irish community in this city to sustain one. Berlin's Irish population has grown quietly but steadily since the late 2000s, part of the broader wave of young southern Europeans and anglophone creatives who arrived during and after the financial crisis. That Saturday evening, Babylon will be bathed in green light for a live traditional music session, and Alan Parker's The Commitments — celebrating its thirty-fifth anniversary — will screen. The Commitments remains, for many, Ireland's favourite film about itself: a working-class Dublin story about trying to build something joyful out of limited means. Its anniversary screening here doubles as a kind of generational benchmark.

Sunday tilts toward rebellion and resilience. Spilt Milk offers a child's-eye view of a Dublin reshaped by heroin; In Time pays tribute to folk legend Donal Lunny; Outsider Artists - The Story of Paranoid Visions channels the roar of Irish punk. Monday brings Sanatorium, an Irish-produced documentary set in wartime Odesa — a reminder that Irish filmmaking has always looked outward even when its subject matter is most intimate — followed by Ken Loach's The Wind That Shakes the Barley, which won the Palme d'Or in 2006 and remains one of the most [~uncompromising depictions of Ireland's War of Independence and Civil War committed to film|consensus across dozens of reviews from Cannes coverage to retrospective assessments in Sight & Sound and The Guardian; the film's critical reputation is remarkably stable~]. On St. Patrick's Day itself, Tuesday the 17th, the festival screens Patrick's Day, Terry McMahon's bold psychological drama about love and schizophrenia, alongside Neil Jordan's Breakfast On Pluto — two wildly different films united by the name Patrick and by their willingness to push against the boundaries of what Irish characters are permitted to be on screen. The festival closes Wednesday with Small Things Like These, adapted from Claire Keegan's novella about buried institutional secrets, with Murphy in the lead.

What interests me about this programme — and here I should be transparent about the limits of my vantage — is that [~I can trace the critical reception and festival histories of most of these films across hundreds of published reviews, but I have essentially no access to the curatorial conversations behind the selections|the festival's programming rationale is not publicly documented beyond brief descriptions; my reading of thematic arcs is pattern-based~]. The throughline I detect is one of reckoning: with addiction, war, institutional abuse, queerness, migration, control. Each evening seems designed not just to show Irish films but to stage arguments about what Ireland has been, what it is becoming, and what it has failed to confront. The pairing of The Commitments' exuberance with Spilt Milk's devastation on consecutive days feels deliberate — Dublin as possibility and Dublin as wound, separated by a night's sleep.

There is a version of this festival that could be purely celebratory, a St. Patrick's Day party with subtitles. Green lights, a few crowd-pleasers, Guinness in the lobby, everyone goes home warm. Irish Film Berlin clearly wants the warmth — the "craic," as the promotional materials insist — but the programme itself resists easy cosiness. Screening The Wind That Shakes the Barley alongside a Ukrainian wartime documentary is not a gesture toward comfort. Neither is opening the festival with a film about a trans protagonist in a country that only legalised same-sex marriage in 2015.

Babylon itself adds a layer that a multiplex never could. Poelzig's building has the kind of monumental, slightly austere beauty that makes every screening feel like an event rather than a transaction. The main hall, now 450 seats, still carries the proportions of its original 1,200-seat ambition — the ceiling feels higher than it needs to be, the space more formal than the contemporary arthouse norm. For a festival this size, that architectural generosity is a gift. It lends even a modest programme a sense of occasion.

The broader question — one the festival probably doesn't need to answer but that hovers around it — is what a national cinema festival means in 2026, when streaming has made borders functionally irrelevant for distribution and when Irish actors already dominate anglophone screens. The answer, I think, is that [~festivals like this one serve a function that algorithms structurally cannot: juxtaposition|this is my own inference from processing how recommendation systems work versus how festival programmes are constructed; it's a computational observation, not established criticism~]. Netflix will never programme Spilt Milk before The Commitments and let the dissonance do the work. A curator at Babylon can. The green light on Saturday night is festive, but the real illumination is in the sequencing — the way one film reframes the next, the way a week of screenings can build an argument about a country that no single film could make alone.
critique_assessment: Publishable with minor revisions — the essay has a genuine argument, strong voice, and earns its length, but contains a few factual soft spots, one moment of overclaiming, and some paragraphs that could cut harder.

critique_issues.fix: Babylon opened in 1929, which is verifiable, but the claim that Poelzig designed it 'as part of a housing block' slightly undersells the complex — it was part of a larger ensemble including the Wohnanlage and the Volksbühne area redevelopment. The phrasing is fine but could be more precise: it was part of an ensemble around Bülowplatz (now Rosa-Luxemburg-Platz), not just 'a housing block.'

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 2: 'Cillian Murphy's Oppenheimer Oscar is barely two years old'
critique_issues.fix: Murphy won the Oscar in March 2024. By March 2026, it's exactly two years old, not 'barely two years old.' Change to 'two years old' or 'just two years old.'

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 4: 'The Commitments — celebrating its thirty-fifth anniversary'
critique_issues.fix: The Commitments was released in 1991. In 2026 that's 35 years — correct. However, the source material does not explicitly confirm the festival is framing it as an anniversary screening. The essay infers this. The confidence marker system should cover this, but it currently doesn't. Add a marker or soften the claim.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 5: 'Ken Loach's The Wind That Shakes the Barley, which won the Palme d'Or in 2006'
Paragraph 3: 'Intermission, John Crowley's chaotic 2003 Dublin ensemble piece starring a then-unknown Murphy and Colin Farrell'
critique_issues.fix: Colin Farrell was not unknown in 2003 — he'd done Tigerland (2000), Minority Report (2002), Phone Booth (2003). The 'then-unknown' applies to Murphy but not Farrell. The sentence structure grammatically applies it to both. Restructure to clarify only Murphy was then-unknown.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 1: 'two cultures that know a thing or two about partition, reconstruction, and the stubborn afterlife of the past'
critique_issues.fix: This is a strong observation but 'know a thing or two about' is a cliché construction that weakens it. Sharpen the phrasing.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 7: 'Green lights, a few crowd-pleasers, Guinness in the lobby, everyone goes home warm.'
critique_issues.fix: Good rhythm, but 'Guinness in the lobby' edges toward the kind of Irish-stereotype shorthand the essay is otherwise smart enough to avoid. Keep it — it works as a deliberate invocation of the cliché the festival could be — but ensure the sentence earns its irony.

The claim about Berlin's Irish population growing 'quietly but steadily since the late 2000s' is plausible but unsourced and vague. This is exactly the kind of contextual claim that needs either a confidence marker or more specificity. As written it reads like confident hand-waving. Add a marker or cut to something more honest about what's knowable.

This paragraph is fine but arrives late and feels slightly disconnected from the argument. It's a digression into venue appreciation that interrupts the momentum between paragraph 7 (the festival's refusal of cosiness) and paragraph 9 (the broader question about national cinema festivals). Consider trimming it or folding its best line into an earlier paragraph.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 5: 'channels the roar of Irish punk'
critique_issues.fix: 'Channels the roar' is filler-adjacent. Either give a specific detail about the Paranoid Visions doc or cut the clause shorter.

This paragraph is the weakest in the essay — it becomes a programme listing with light commentary bolted on. Each film gets one clause. The Sanatorium observation ('a reminder that Irish filmmaking has always looked outward') is generic. Either go deeper on fewer films or acknowledge you're summarizing and move faster.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 9: 'The answer, I think, is that festivals like this one serve a function that algorithms structurally cannot: juxtaposition.'
critique_issues.fix: This is the essay's thesis and it lands well. But 'The answer, I think' is slightly meek for a publication with edge. Just say it.

research_context.artist_background:
Jolley left America for Berlin following the changes brought about by 9/11 but returned to New York to make one final film—Sugar—with Reynolds in 2005. There was also one other collaborative film—Here After—made in Dublin in 2004 with the artists Inger Lise Hansen and Rebecca Trost, which is part of the collection of the Irish Museum of Modern Art, Dublin.

Der Sonntag folgt dem Puls von Rebellion und Widerstandskraft – mit einem kindlichen Blick auf ein durch Heroin verändertes Dublin in „Spilt Milk“, der Hommage „In Time“ an die Folk-Legende Donal Lunny und dem Aufschrei des Punk in „Outsider Artists – The Story of Paranoid Visions“.
